title: The one who hides
hook: the hymn's five acts of the goddess, and two of them are hiding and grace
carry: hiding is hers, and so is grace
tomorrow: a jeweled city, and a second address inside the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama told a war in names, and ended it with Kama, love, brought back from ash.

A baby on a kitchen floor, and a grown-up behind a dish towel. The towel goes up, the face is gone, and the baby goes still, a little worried. The towel comes down, there's the face again, and the baby shrieks with laughter. Peekaboo only works because of the hiding: without the moment of not-seeing, there's nothing to find. Today the Lalita Sahasranama does something like it on a cosmic scale. In a short run of names, it lists what the goddess does with the whole universe. Some of it is expected. Two of the acts are not.
screen: `A FACE BEHIND A DISH TOWEL.` → `NO HIDING, NOTHING TO FIND.` → `WHAT SHE DOES WITH THE UNIVERSE.`

segments.voice: Here is the run, in paraphrase. She is the maker, in the form of Brahma. The protector, in the form of Govinda, a name of Vishnu. The one who draws everything back in, in the form of Rudra. The one who conceals, as Ishvara, the Lord. She is Sadashiva, the giver of grace. And a name gathers them up: she is devoted to the five acts. Making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing and grace. Two things stand out. First, the great gods appear as forms the goddess takes. In Shaiva traditions the same five acts belong to Shiva; in this hymn to the goddess they are hers, and the gods are her ways of doing them. Second, after withdrawal comes concealment. The Sanskrit is tirodhana: hiding, veiling. Some teachers who use this list say it's the act that makes the world seem to be only itself, so the deeper reality behind it is out of sight. Then the last act: anugraha, grace, favor, the turning toward someone. The towel coming down. Some readers take the order seriously: concealing comes before grace, the way hiding comes before finding. Either way, here's the teaching. When God feels far away, this tradition doesn't read it as God gone. Hiding is one of her own acts, and grace is on the same list. Devotees in a dry season of prayer lean on that: the distance is hers too, and so is the turning back. The one who hides is the one who reveals.
screen: `MAKING, KEEPING, WITHDRAWING.` · `THE GODS AS HER FORMS.` · `CONCEALING: TIRODHANA.` · `GRACE: ANUGRAHA.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO HIDES IS THE ONE WHO REVEALS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a few breaths and let the room be concealed: the chair, the walls, the light are all still there, you just can't see them. Then slowly open your eyes and let the room come back, as if it were being handed to you; close them and rest, open them and receive, each opening unhurried. If you pray, you can greet the goddess in what returns, in your own words; if you don't, just notice what it's like to be given the room again.
The Lalita Sahasranama. Today, its five acts of the goddess: making, keeping, withdrawing, concealing, and grace.
Your line: hiding is hers, and so is grace. The one who hides is the one who reveals. Until tomorrow.
